lead: A key is a small piece of metal that sits in a groove cut in the shaft and in the hub of a gear, pulley or coupling. It locks the two parts so the shaft can drive the hub without slipping. A spline does the same job with many teeth, so it carries more torque. Keys allow quick assembly and repair. You meet them in every electric motor, pump, gearbox and bicycle crank. Their size is small, but a failed key stops the whole machine.
prereq: You need: torsion and shear stress from Chapter 3.1, and fits and crushing stress from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A keyway is the slot cut in the shaft and in the hub. The key sits in the slot. A sunk key is partly in the shaft and partly in the hub; it is the common rectangular or square key. A square key has width w equal to height h. A saddle key sits on the shaft surface and depends on friction; use it for light loads. A round key is a short pin in a drilled hole; it locates a part or carries small torque. A spline is a set of many keys cut as teeth on the shaft.

items: Sunk key: rectangular or square, slots in shaft and hub.
Saddle key: no shaft slot, friction drive, light duty.
Round key: drilled hole, small torque or location.
Spline: many teeth, high torque, sliding hub possible.

blocks.text: Key material is usually mild steel for light duty and alloy steel for high torque. The key must be snug sideways in the keyway, with a small top clearance for a sunk key so the hub can sit on the shaft shoulder. Standard tables link shaft diameter to key width and height. Check the table in the design handbook before choosing a key.

sections.h3: Force and stresses in a rectangular key

blocks.text: Torque T on the shaft is passed to the key at the shaft surface. The tangential force F acts at radius d/2, so T = F d/2. Here T is torque in N·mm, F is force in N, and d is shaft diameter in mm. If power P in W and speed N in rpm are given, first find T = P × 60/(2πN) with T in N·m, then convert to N·mm.

blocks.where: T is torque in N·mm; F is tangential force on the key in N; d is shaft diameter in mm.

blocks.text: The key fails in two ways. It may shear across the plane between shaft and hub. The shear area is w L, so τ = F/(w L). It may crush on the side that bears against the keyway. Only half the key height is in the hub, so the crushing area is (h/2) L and σ<sub>c</sub> = F/(h L/2). Here w is key width in mm, h is key height in mm, L is effective key length in mm, τ is shear stress in N/mm² or MPa, and σ<sub>c</sub> is crushing stress in MPa. Check both against allowable values.

blocks.where: τ is shear stress in MPa; F is tangential force in N; w is key width in mm; L is key length in mm.
σ<sub>c</sub> is crushing stress in MPa; F is tangential force in N; h is key height in mm; L is key length in mm.

blocks.text: The keyway cuts the shaft section and adds sharp corners. That raises stress in torsion and fatigue. A shaft with one keyway is weaker than a plain shaft of the same diameter; design handbooks give a factor to allow for this. Do not use the full shaft diameter without allowance when a keyway is present.

sections.h3: Splines and keyway effect on the shaft

blocks.text: Splines are many keys cut as teeth. A straight-sided spline has parallel sides; an involute spline has curved flanks like a gear tooth. Both let a hub slide along the shaft while carrying torque; gearbox sliding gears use this. Load per tooth is lower than a single key. Detailed spline stress analysis is taught in only a few universities; most syllabi stop at the idea of many-key joints. The keyway root is a stress raiser. Use a fillet at the corner where possible. For a single keyway, a common design check is to reduce the shaft's torsional strength by about one-fifth. This is a design allowance, not a precise rule; follow the handbook value for the corner radius and material.

figure.caption: The tree groups key types. Sunk keys may be rectangular or square, and splines may be straight or involute; a spline is a many-key joint.

examples.question: A 50 mm diameter shaft transmits 20 kW at 600 rpm through a rectangular key 14 mm wide by 9 mm high and 70 mm long. The key material has allowable shear stress 40 MPa and allowable crushing stress 80 MPa. Check the key for shear and crushing.
steps: Shear area A<sub>s</sub> = w L = 14 × 70 = 980 mm². Shear stress τ = F/A<sub>s</sub> = 12,732.4/980 = 12.99 MPa. This is less than 40 MPa, so the key is safe in shear.
Crushing area A<sub>c</sub> = (h/2) L = (9/2) × 70 = 315 mm². Crushing stress σ<sub>c</sub> = F/A<sub>c</sub> = 12,732.4/315 = 40.42 MPa. This is less than 80 MPa, so the key is safe in crushing.
examples.answer: The key is safe: shear stress is 12.99 MPa (limit 40 MPa) and crushing stress is 40.42 MPa (limit 80 MPa).
examples.check:
import math
P = 20000.0
N = 600.0
d = 50.0
w = 14.0
h = 9.0
L = 70.0
omega = 2 * math.pi * N / 60
T_Nm = P / omega
T_Nmm = T_Nm * 1000
F = 2 * T_Nmm / d
tau = F / (w * L)
sigma_c = F / (L * h / 2)
print(f"{T_Nmm:.0f}")
print(f"{F:.1f}")
print(f"{tau:.2f}")
print(f"{sigma_c:.2f}")

traps: Using the full key height h in crushing. The bearing area is hL/2, because the key bears on half its height in the hub and half in the shaft.
Taking key force as T/d. The force acts at the shaft surface, so F = T/(d/2) = 2T/d.
Forgetting the keyway. A keyway removes material and adds a sharp corner, so the shaft is weaker in torsion than a plain shaft.
Checking only shear. A key often fails by crushing first; check both shear and crushing.
Using a key length longer than the hub. The effective length is the contact length in the hub, not the total length of the key.

quiz.a: Sunk key (rectangular or square), saddle key, round key, and spline.

quiz.q: Why is a saddle key used only for light loads?
quiz.a: A saddle key has no slot in the shaft. It relies on friction between the key and the shaft surface. Friction can slip under high torque or vibration, so it is limited to light duty.

quiz.q: A 40 mm shaft transmits 10 kW at 900 rpm. The key is 12 mm wide and 50 mm long. Find the shear stress in the key. Use F = 2T/d.
Why does a keyway reduce shaft fatigue strength even if the key itself is strong enough?
quiz.a: The keyway removes material from the shaft section and leaves sharp corners. Sharp corners raise the local stress. Under repeated torsion or bending, the raised stress starts a fatigue crack at the keyway root, so the shaft fails before a plain shaft of the same diameter.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a spline?
quiz.a: A spline carries torque between a shaft and a hub using many teeth. It can also let the hub slide along the shaft while still transmitting torque.

quiz.q: Explain why the crushing area of a sunk key uses h/2, not the full height h.
quiz.a: A sunk key is half in the shaft and half in the hub. Each side bears on a height of h/2. The crushing stress is checked on that bearing area, so the area is L × h/2.

quiz.q: A square key has width and height 10 mm and length 60 mm. The tangential force is 8000 N. Find the shear stress and the crushing stress.
quiz.a: Shear area = wL = 10 × 60 = 600 mm². τ = 8000/600 = 13.33 MPa. Crushing area = (h/2)L = 5 × 60 = 300 mm². σc = 8000/300 = 26.67 MPa.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, key and spline sizes come from standard tables, and designers check the shaft with a stress-concentration factor from handbooks. Splines are common in automotive gearboxes and aircraft transmissions, where many teeth share the load. Newer curricula add finite element analysis of keyways and spline roots. Search for spline joint design, keyway stress concentration factor, and involute spline standard.
